name: Befang
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Abre (Unjidi), Charles. 2003. The phonology of Bifaŋ [Befang]. Maîtrise dissertation, Department of African Languages and Linguistics, Université de Yaoundé I (supervisor Bitjaa Kody Zachée Denis). vi+100 pp. MPI Language Description Heritage, hdl:11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7F32-6.
catalog_quote: Befang is a tone language. A tone language is one that uses tones to distinguish meaning in words. [...] The Befang language has four basic tones. Two level tones; high and low, abbreviated (H, L), and two contour tones which are the falling tone (ˆ) or (HL) and the rising tone (ˇ) or (LH). The contour tones in this language are derived from floating tones docking on the adjacent tone bearing unit (TBU). These floating tones result from vowel deletion or from vowels which devocalise as glides. Before we get into the proper examination of the tone system of Befang, it will be worth noting that, this language has some words, which are tonologically identical but differ in meaning. In such cases, it is the context that determines the word the speaker is actually referring to.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible phonology says Befang is a lexical tone language with H, L and derived HL/LH contour tones; it contains no statement of any kind about word stress, accent or prominence, so no stress rule can be attributed to the language from this source.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress discussion at all). The thesis notes tonally identical homophones distinguished only by context (p. 70) and phonemic vowel length (p. 68).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone on nouns and verbs (citation forms from a ~1200-word elicited list, Befang and Okomanjang dialects, informants in Yaoundé and Befang village). Nothing on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Abre 2003 describes 'Bifaŋ/Befang' proper, with Okomanjang treated as a second dialect of the same language (pp. 13-14); Gueche Fotso 2004 covers Befang. Asohsi 2015/16 describes the Obang dialect (Glottolog maps Obang to befa1241/bby); Boum 1981 describes Modele, which Ethnologue/Wikipedia list as the Modele-Ushaku dialect of the same language. No separate glottocodes exist for these dialects in Glottolog 5.1.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Befang is described as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (HL, LH), the contours arising from floating tones docking on the adjacent TBU after vowel deletion or gliding. The dissertation says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence: a full-text search for stress/accent the whole text for stress / accent / prominence / prosody / intonation / rhythm / weight finds only the acute and grave 'accent' tone-mark diacritics (p. 71) and the phrase 'tone.. a prosodic feature' (p. 69); the only 'light syllable' mention (p. 68) is about disallowed VV sequences, not prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; p. 70 notes tonologically identical homophones disambiguated by context
new_statements.identity_note: Abre 2003 covers the Befang and Okomanjang dialects (pp. 13-14), which it treats as one language; its classification chart (p. 11) places it Western Grassfields > Menchum > Befang (ALCAM 851), matching Glottolog befa1241 / ISO 639-3 bby. The work's title spelling 'Bifaŋ' is the author's own name for Befang, not a different variety. The Glottolog citation form 'Unjidi, Charles' is the same author as 'Abre Charles Unjidi' on the title page.
